Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 4.4 ('Attribute Accumulation'), stating that 'typical continuous attributes can be blended, whereas cardinal ones... cannot' and providing the specific formulas for z-pass (replacement based on weight, effectively max-weight for cardinal) and z-blend (weighted addition for continuous, max-weight comparison for cardinal). The mention of the $ eta$-band is also supported by the description of the ternary depth test in Section 4.3, which defines the $ eta$-band for z-blend operations.

If $w_d < w_f$, replace destination with source; otherwise keep destination [S1]:

The claim states that for cardinal attributes, if the destination weight ($w_d$) is less than the source weight ($w_f$), the destination is replaced with the source; otherwise, the destination is kept. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the notes section ('On z-blend, for cardinal attributes, compare destination weight wd and source weight wf. If wd < wf, replace with source; otherwise keep destination.') and in the main text/Table 4 context which describes cardinal attributes as not being blended but rather compared/replaced based on weight. The mathematical notation provided in the notes $(w_d, a_d) := (w_f, a_s)$ if $w_d < w_f$, else $(w_d, a_d)$ directly matches the claim.
